mechanism: A free Telegram signals group is funded by an introducing-broker deal: members are steered to open accounts with a partner broker, and the broker pays the group a rebate per lot traded, win or lose. The group's income therefore depends on member trading volume, not on signal accuracy. The FCA answers this model with an unauthorised-firm warning once it sees promotion of regulated activity without authorisation, and the broker's rebate flow is the paper trail.

why_not_testable: It is a live promotional funnel; nothing can be run from here without joining it, and the vault wants it understood, not operated.
one_line: Free signals groups earn per lot traded by members, so they profit from volume whether members win or lose; the FCA warning is the regulator's answer.
idea_why: Pay-per-lot incentives reward churn, not accuracy, so the model is structurally misaligned with members.
breakdown: To study it, read the FCA warning list and the register entries for named firms, then compare the group's claimed win rate against any public signal history. Broker rebate structures are documented in introducing-broker terms published by brokers. A hired analyst would check the register, archive the channel's posted signals and score them against public gold price data to see whether the claims hold. Nothing here needs operating the scheme.

mechanism: A proposer model builds search tasks answer-first from unlabeled questions, working back to an evidence path so each task is validated. A solver is trained with reinforcement learning on those tasks. The proposer is rewarded for tasks of intermediate difficulty for the current solver, and the solver gets a reward that penalises redundant searches among correct answers.
claim: Zero-label co-evolution training improves search agents' accuracy and tool efficiency on seven QA benchmarks.
why_not_testable: It needs RL training of a language model, and there is no local LLM or GPU here.
needs: GPU training and a base model
one_line: Search agents can be trained with no labels: one model invents tasks at the solver's edge, and the solver is rewarded for fewer searches.
idea_why: The reward design is plausible but the gains rest on benchmark numbers that only a training run would confirm.
breakdown: Start from a question set, have a proposer generate answer-first tasks with checked evidence paths, then train a small open model with RL using the two rewards. Public QA benchmarks give evaluation. A researcher with GPU time would do the training; no script here covers it.

mechanism: A model compiles a dataset-search query into a typed plan, and only deterministic operators execute it over hybrid retrieval and bounded graph expansion. Evidence is checked against provenance before a ranking is accepted, and failures yield a typed diagnosis allowing local repairs. The point is that the model that picks a dataset does not also declare it a match.
claim: On HuDS-Bench (200 queries), NDCG@10 rises 25.7 percent over the best hybrid and 18.9 percent over a commercial agent.
why_not_testable: It needs an LLM for plan compilation and a large dataset index; no local model.
needs: An LLM key or local model and the benchmark index
one_line: A dataset-search agent where the model only writes typed plans and plain code checks the evidence, so it cannot mark its own homework.
idea_why: Separating the model's proposals from deterministic verification is a well-founded pattern for constraint-heavy search.
breakdown: Define a small schema for search plans, write operators over a dataset metadata index, and have the model emit plans only in that schema. Verification code checks each constraint such as licence or task against recorded metadata. The repo and benchmark are public, so a reproduction starts there.
